document_title: The Sky Has No State Rule. The Ground Does Now.
post_copy:
Drones seeded clouds over Kachemak Bay on August 23rd. On October 20th the Kenai Peninsula Borough's pending seeding rule passed 7 to 0.

In the sky, two drones Rainmaker calls autonomous released 19 flares with about 374 grams of silver iodide.
On the ground, the borough found out from Rainmaker's press release.

In the sky, no state rule applies and no DEC permit was needed.
On the ground, seeding from borough land needs a lease or permit and ten disclosures down to each flare's serial number.

Inside are the night of the flights, the payload, a radar estimate against a rain gauge, each government's own words and the ten-line form.

The borough asked the Legislature to ban cloud seeding or require a permit. Its ten disclosures are the right start. Should a state permit stop at those ten or need a yes from the borough under the flight?

#KenaiPeninsula #CloudSeeding #AKleg

slides.headline: The sky has no state rule. The ground does now.
Two drones seeded the clouds. The borough answered.
slides.body: On August 23rd Rainmaker flew two drones it calls autonomous from near the head of Kachemak Bay. On October 20th the borough Assembly voted 7 to 0, two absent, to require a lease or permit for weather modification on borough land.

slides.headline: 19 flares. 374 grams of silver iodide.
slides.body: Each red flare dispersed about 19.7 grams. The new form asks every applicant for each flare's quantity, type, manufacturer, serial number and total weight, plus a safety data sheet for anything released.

slides.headline: Radar saw it. The water was modeled.
slides.body: Rainmaker's report puts the first radar signature 40.4 minutes after release, during seven seeding missions between 0618 and 0954 UTC. DEC calls the result a modeled estimate, not a measurement of water collected at the ground.

slides.headline: 19 million gallons. About 0.01 inches.
slides.body: Rainmaker puts the added precipitation at 57.62 acre-feet across 249.53 square kilometers, with a range of 41.70 to 89.35. Spread over that area, Rainmaker says, it's about a hundredth of an inch.

slides.headline: 0954 UTC. Seeding ends.
slides.body: Nobody needed a state permit to start.

slides.headline: Whose sky is it?
slides.body:
Reporting, not a comprehensive permitting program, DEC says.
No DEC permit required. No framework specific to weather modification. DNR sent a letter of no objection.
Can't fully regulate weather modification or airspace, its legal memo says. So it ruled its own land.

slides.headline: Before seeding from borough land, name the outcome. Then list ten things.
slides.body: Skip the signed closeout and it's $1,000 a day, plus a 5-year ban.
labels: 3 FLARES BY QUANTITY, TYPE, MANUFACTURER, SERIAL NUMBER, WEIGHT
7 DURATION AND ALTITUDE OF EACH FLIGHT
10 RELEASE COORDINATES AND PREDICTED IMPACT AREAS

slides.headline: Which should Alaska choose?
slides.body: The borough asked the Legislature to ban cloud seeding or require a permit.

aftercare: Post in a Tuesday to Thursday slot, 8 to 11 a.m. Alaska time. Tuesday, October 27th is the first such slot after this draft. When to post is the owner's call.

Paste the sources comment within 60 seconds of posting and pin it. The two Legistar API links are long raw URLs, so click each one after posting, and if LinkedIn cuts one short the full text is still there to copy.
Before publishing, check that the PDF document title reads "The Sky Has No State Rule. The Ground Does Now."

Reply to every comment in the first 60 to 90 minutes. Expect Homer and House District 6 readers, since Rep. Sarah Vance says she'll sponsor a weather modification bill if re-elected. No bill text exists, so don't describe what it would do, and don't take a side in the race.

Answer the three likely misreadings from the record. Safety, DEC found no evidence of adverse impact from these activities and said that is not a ruling on future seeding. AI, the record says autonomous, which is Rainmaker's word, and no Rainmaker page mentions AI. A ban, the rule covers borough land only and bans seeding outright only on casual-use borough land.
After 48 hours, note saves, comments and reposts for the ledger.
editor_notes_for_email:
Three things to watch. (1) 57.62 acre-feet and 19 million gallons are Rainmaker's radar estimate (C46, C51); DEC calls such figures modeled estimates (C73), and the 0.01 inches is Rainmaker's own conversion as DEC relays it (C38), which slide 05 now attributes to Rainmaker. (2) 'Autonomous' is Rainmaker's word (C52); nothing in the deck or the caption says AI. (3) The rule covers borough land only, through leases and land use permits (C08, C25); the caption's 'no state rule applies' rests on DEC's 'no regulatory framework specific to weather modification' (C34). Slide 08 runs past the 50-word budget on purpose because it carries the full ten-row list. Slide 04's body was tightened by the showrunner for layout (same claims). The ADN editorial of September 12th is left out of the first comment because claims.json gives no URL for it.
PRIOR COVERAGE: No.64 (September 20th) covered Ordinance 2026-35 as a draft. This deck reports its enactment; the hook calls it the borough's pending seeding rule. If you want returning readers to see it as an update in plain words, add a first-comment line pointing to the September 20th deck. Slide 09 asks ban or permit (the borough's own request to the Legislature); the caption's closing fork is narrower (a disclosure-only state permit or one that also needs the borough's yes). Pick one for replies.
